hints: Focus on what happens to chlorine in sodium hydroxide, it disproportionates into chloride and another oxochlorate ion.
Remember that both cold and hot NaOH give $\text{NaCl}$ as one product, only the other product changes from $\text{ClO}^-$ to $\text{ClO}_3^-$.
Consider reactivity of halogens for statement 3, a more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive one from its salt to form a new chloride salt.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1, chlorine with cold NaOH**

Chlorine disproportionates in cold dilute alkali. Chloride is always one of the products.

$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH(cold)} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check statement 2, chlorine with hot NaOH**

With hot concentrated alkali the disproportionation goes further, but chloride is still formed.

$$3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH(hot)} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check statement 3, chlorine with NaBr**

Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from aqueous bromide.

$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaBr} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl} + \text{Br}_2$$

**Combine the conclusions**

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. $\text{NaCl}$ is a product in all three reactions.

options.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all true. Cold NaOH gives NaCl + NaClO, hot NaOH gives NaCl + NaClO3, and displacement of Br- by Cl2 gives NaCl + Br2.
options.B: Incorrect. This option suggests only 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is also correct because chlorine oxidises bromide to bromine, forming sodium chloride.
options.C: Incorrect. This option leaves out statement 1. Statement 1 is definitely correct as shown by the cold disproportionation equation producing NaCl.
options.D: Incorrect. This option includes only statement 1. Both statements 2 and 3 are also correct, so limiting to statement 1 alone is wrong.
